name: Python for Data
summary: NumPy arrays and pandas DataFrames are the workhorses for loading, slicing and summarising data in Python.
key_points: NumPy arrays support fast vectorised maths without loops
A pandas DataFrame is a table with labelled rows and columns
Boolean masks and groupby let you filter and summarise data
analogy: Think of a DataFrame as a spreadsheet you can program.
common_mistake: Looping over rows when a vectorised operation would be shorter and much faster.

name: Linear Algebra Basics
summary: Vectors and matrices represent data and transformations; dot products and matrix multiplication combine them.
key_points: A vector is an ordered list of numbers; a matrix is a grid of numbers
The dot product multiplies matching entries and sums them
Matrix multiplication needs matching inner dimensions: (m x n)(n x p) gives m x p
analogy: A matrix is a machine that stretches, rotates or mixes the inputs you feed it.
common_mistake: Multiplying matrices with incompatible shapes, or assuming A.B equals B.A.

name: Calculus and Derivatives
summary: A derivative measures how fast a function changes; the chain rule handles functions built from other functions.
key_points: The derivative of f at x is the slope of the tangent line
Power rule: d/dx of x^n is n times x^(n-1)
Chain rule: d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) times g'(x)
analogy: The derivative is the speedometer reading of a function at a single instant.
common_mistake: Forgetting to multiply by the inner derivative when applying the chain rule.

name: Probability Basics
summary: Probability quantifies uncertainty; conditional probability and Bayes' rule update beliefs as evidence arrives.
key_points: Probabilities lie between 0 and 1, and the outcomes of an experiment sum to 1
For independent events P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B)
Bayes' rule: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B)
analogy: A probability is a degree of belief that gets revised each time you see new evidence.

name: Data Preprocessing
summary: Raw data must be cleaned, encoded and scaled before a model can learn from it.
key_points: Handle missing values by dropping or imputing them
Encode categories as numbers, for example one-hot encoding
Scale features so that large-valued columns do not dominate
analogy: Preprocessing is washing and chopping vegetables before you cook.
common_mistake: Fitting the scaler on the full dataset, which leaks test information into training.

name: Linear Regression
summary: Linear regression fits a line (or hyperplane) that predicts a number by minimising the squared error.
key_points: The prediction is y_hat = w.x + b
The loss is the mean squared error between predictions and targets
Weights can be found with the normal equation or with gradient descent
analogy: You are drawing the straight line that sits closest to all the points.
common_mistake: Reading a high R-squared as proof of causation or that the model is correct.

name: Gradient Descent
summary: Gradient descent minimises a loss by repeatedly stepping opposite to the gradient.
key_points: Update rule: w <- w - eta times the gradient of the loss
The learning rate eta controls the step size
Too large a rate diverges; too small a rate is slow
analogy: Walking downhill in fog: you feel the slope under your feet and step downhill.
common_mistake: Using a learning rate so large that the loss bounces up instead of down.

name: Logistic Regression
summary: Logistic regression predicts the probability of a class by passing a linear score through the sigmoid function.
key_points: Sigmoid(z) = 1/(1+e^-z) maps any number into (0,1)
The decision threshold is usually 0.5 on the predicted probability
It is trained by minimising log loss (cross-entropy)
analogy: A linear score is squashed into a probability, like a dimmer switch between 0 and 1.
common_mistake: Treating the output as a class label instead of a probability.

name: Model Evaluation
summary: Evaluation measures how well a model generalises to unseen data using held-out splits and suitable metrics.
key_points: Precision = TP/(TP+FP); recall = TP/(TP+FN)
Accuracy misleads on imbalanced classes
Cross-validation averages performance over several train/validation splits
analogy: Evaluation is the mock exam with questions you have not seen before.
common_mistake: Reporting accuracy on the training set, or tuning on the test set.

name: Overfitting and Regularization
summary: An overfit model memorises training noise; regularization penalises complexity to improve generalization.
key_points: Overfitting: low training error but high validation error
L2 (ridge) adds lambda times the sum of squared weights; L1 (lasso) adds lambda times the sum of absolute weights and can zero weights
A larger lambda means stronger regularization and a simpler model
analogy: Regularization is a budget on how wiggly the curve is allowed to be.
common_mistake: Setting lambda so high that the model underfits.

name: Neural Network Basics
summary: A neural network stacks layers of weighted sums followed by non-linear activations.
key_points: A neuron computes an activation of (w.x + b)
Non-linear activations such as ReLU let the network model non-linear patterns
Layers are matrix multiplications, so shapes must line up
analogy: Each layer re-describes the data in a form that is easier for the next layer to separate.
common_mistake: Stacking layers without non-linear activations, which collapses to one linear layer.

name: Backpropagation
summary: Backpropagation applies the chain rule layer by layer to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight.
key_points: A forward pass computes the outputs and the loss
A backward pass multiplies local derivatives from the output back to each weight
The resulting gradients feed a gradient descent update
analogy: It is like passing blame backwards: each layer is told how much it contributed to the final error.
common_mistake: Forgetting to keep the forward-pass values that the backward pass needs.
